why_interesting: The problem's 'Data Representation' dimension (how information is encoded, stored and transported) is where the conventional approach carries a structural assumption: The representation is uniform across the whole tensor or molecule, so a few significant elements pay for many insignificant ones. AARL took a mechanism that already works in photonics, neuromorphic engineering, analog computing, condensed matter physics - Change the physical carrier that performs the operation instead of optimising the existing carrier further. - and asked what happens if it is applied to GPU. If the mechanism transfers, the gain would come from removing that assumption rather than from tuning the existing design. Whether it transfers is exactly what is not established here.

first_experiment.objective: Establish whether the mechanism moves information density per unit cost for GPU at all, before tuning anything.
first_experiment.design: Baseline A: the conventional data representation approach. Variant B: the Substrate substitution mechanism applied only to the data representation dimension. Keep every other parameter identical and use the same seed/warm-up.
first_experiment.decision_rule: Only claim support if B moves information density per unit cost outside the run-to-run spread of A; if the spread is larger than the effect, report INCONCLUSIVE rather than a direction.
first_experiment.what_would_make_it_stop: If A is already at the physical or structural limit of information density per unit cost, the comparison cannot discriminate and the design must change.
